chunks: 4753 - And in the narration of al-Naḍr ibn Suwayd, from ʿAbdullāh ibn Sinān, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said:
About a man who said: “His wife is divorced and his slaves are free if I ever drink anything forbidden, or anything lawful, from al-ṭilāʾ, ever.”

So he said: “As for what is forbidden, then he must never approach it, whether he swore an oath or whether he did not swear. And as for al-ṭilāʾ, he has no right to forbid what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has made lawful. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said:”
“O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?”
“So no oath is valid in forbidding what is lawful, nor in making lawful what is forbidden, nor in severing kinship ties.”

key_terms.أَحَلَّ: made lawful or permitted by Allah
key_terms.الطِّلَاءُ: a drink mentioned here as an example of something a person may not forbid upon himself if Allah has made it lawful
key_terms.الْحَرَامُ: that which is forbidden by Allah and must be avoided regardless of personal vows
key_terms.قَطِيعَةِ رَحِمٍ: the severing of family and kinship ties

ai.seo_question: Can an oath make a lawful thing forbidden or a forbidden thing lawful in Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith establishes that a person cannot, by oath or declaration, make lawful things unlawful or unlawful things lawful. It also affirms that the forbidden remains forbidden regardless of any oath, and that oaths involving the severing of kinship have no validity. By citing the Qur’anic address to the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, the narration grounds this legal principle in divine revelation.
